response.query: How can we translate the five repertoire elements into an explicit DAG linking each to mediators (affect, boundary work), confounders, and short- and long-term outcomes?
response.answer: The five repertoire elements link to mediators like affect and boundary work, confounders, and outcomes via a directed acyclic graph (DAG) that shows causal pathways from elements to mediators, confounders, and both short- and long-term outcomes. Mediators explain how elements affect outcomes, while confounders distort these relationships. The DAG clarifies these relationships for analysis.

results.title: How to Measure Short-Term and Long-Term Outcomes
results.content: # How do you measure short-term and long-term outcomes in a program evaluation plan? In this article, you will learn how to measure short-term and long-term outcomes in a program evaluation plan, and why they are important for improving your program performance and accountability. Long-term outcomes are the ultimate or final changes that occur among the program participants or beneficiaries or the broader community or society as a result of the program intervention. To measure long-term outcomes, you need to identify the indicators that capture the specific changes you want to achieve, and collect data from the program participants or beneficiaries or other sources, such as official statistics, reports, or studies, using appropriate methods, such as surveys, interviews, assessments, or evaluations. Long-term outcomes help you evaluate the impact and sustainability of your program, and show the contribution and significance of your program to your mission and vision. The ultimate goal of measuring short-term and long-term outcomes is to use them for program improvement.

results.title: Confounders, mediators, moderators and covariates – A blog about statistical musings
results.content: # Confounders, mediators, moderators and covariates. I started looking for some nice examples that would describe what a mediator was. Of course, it was also important to pre-empt confusion between similar and related terms, and since mediators and confounders are regularly mixed up I also looked for nice examples of confounders. For completeness I looked for examples of moderators and covariates. Mediators and confounders are similar except for the direction of effect between them and the exposure/treatment. Mediators are additionally characterised by lying on the causal pathway between exposure and outcome. Moderators are simply interaction terms that change the size or direction (or both) of the effect of the exposure on outcome. The confusion between mediators and confounders arises from the fact that both have associations between the exposure and outcome. 1. results.title: Simple examples to understand what confounders, colliders, mediators, and moderators are and how to “control for” variables in R with regression and propensity-score matching | R-bloggers
results.content: To conclude, you always have to think about whether there might be factors that affect BOTH your X and Y of interest, and include them in an analysis – if you don’t have data from a randomized experiment (no control variables needed there usually) but rather from observational studies. Again: Saying that children in the household doesn’t actually affect your household income, because the effect disappears when you control for working hours, would be wrong – X *does* affect Y via the mediator variable. By contrast, in the vaccination example, if we control for the confounders (age etc.) and find no direct effect anymore, then we would say that there is in fact apparently no causal effect from X on Y. Example: If you run a regression with the above data – *summary(lm(e~x,d))* – you will find that an additional child lowers your income on average by 261 Euros, and this effect is statistically significant. Showing both models with and without the mediator variable lets you (and your audience) quickly recognize that, first, having children is in general associated with lower income, and, second, the effect is caused by parents working fewer hours. If you have multiple variables and a more complex model, you can include an interaction effect into a regression or ANOVA to see if there is a moderator effect (e.g., gender \* working hours). Let’s look at a new example: Assume we have a study among school children aged 6 to 17 and we want to assess whether there is an effect of exercising on the resting heart rate. set.seed(2022) age <- sample(6:17, 200, T) exercise <- abs(2*(age/max(age) + rnorm(200,0,1))+1) heart_rate <- 85+(6*12/11) - age*(12/11) - exercise/max(exercise)*0.8 + rnorm(200,0,5) dat <- data.frame(age, exercise, heart_rate) ggplot(dat, aes(x=exercise, y=heart_rate)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method="lm") + theme_classic() + ggtitle("Resting heart rate by physical activity among school children") + xlab("Exercise (hours/week)") + ylab("Resting heart rate (bpm)"). mdat <- match.data(m1) ggplot(mdat, aes(x=factor(fertility_below_2), y=co2)) + geom_boxplot() + geom_jitter(width=.1) + stat_summary(fun.y = "mean", geom = "point", pch="-", size=20, colour = "red") + ylab("CO2 emissions in t") + theme_minimal() + scale_x_discrete(name="Fertility rate", labels=c("more than 2 children", "fewer than 2 children")) t.test(co2 ~ fertility_below_2, mdat).

results.title: Smart investment in climate adaptation by linking the short and long term | Deltares
results.content: Together with Rijkswaterstaat and the Delta Programme Commissioner, Deltares has developed a new method for this: DAPP-Δ, which helps policymakers understand which choices are decisive for the future. By making this interconnection explicit, DAPP-Δ helps to identify strategic choices that maintain flexibility in the future and contribute to an adaptive design of the region. Linking forward-looking adaptation paths and backward-looking paths from future scenarios provides insight into decisive decisions. It thus provides insight into which choices open up or close off certain future scenarios. It also provides insight into the connection between future scenarios and decision points in the shorter term. > For us as asset managers, this method helps us to better link investment choices to long-term developments and to discuss them with the Ministry of Infrastructure and Water Management. The new method helps to better view short- and long-term tasks in context and to clarify the connections between choices in certain regions.

results.title: The Rockefeller University » Scientists discover brain region linking short-term to long-term memory
results.content: ## Scientists discover brain region linking short-term to long-term memory. Now, a new study00167-8) identifies the anterior thalamus as a brain region linking hippocampus and cortex that is key to the memory consolidation process. “The findings provide traction toward understanding how transient memories reorganize across the brain to progressively more enduring forms,” says Rockefeller’s Priya Rajasethupathy. In order to figure out what happens between the hippocampus’ short-term work and the cortex’s long-term pay-off, scientists would need to record the intervening parts of an active, thinking brain over many weeks. “The key was that the mice could learn all three outcomes in the short-term—very high rewarding, low rewarding, and adverse—but only the high reward would be remembered a month out, because it was the most salient memory,” says Josue Regalado, a PhD student in Rajasethupathy’s lab and co-author of the study. The team found that the brain’s anterior thalamus appears to referee memory-consolidating interactions between the hippocampus and the cortex. While Rajasethupathy found this surprising—”the anterior thalamus hasn’t been a prominent part of memory consolidation models”—the finding also made some sense. In two subsequent experiments, Rajasethupathy’s team found that inhibiting the thalamus disrupts the formation of long-term memories in mice and, conversely, boosting the thalamus takes memories that would not have otherwise been stored long-term, and makes them last. “One of the major breakthroughs of this paper is that we show that manipulating the anterior thalamus is one way to increase the importance of a memory, and make the mice store it long-term.”. Future work from Rajasethupathy’s lab will investigate how exactly the thalamus contributes to long-term memory storage. “The question is what the thalamus does when a memory is valuable, and needs to be saved long-term, that it doesn’t do for less valuable memories,” she says. Rajasethupathy suspects that the thalamus provides regular reminders to the cortex until a memory goes from short-term to long-term. “We don’t think the thalamus is the only region needed for memory consolidation, and we hope our findings will be blended with other models out there describing this intervening region,” she says. Anteromedial Thalamus Gates the Selection & Stabilization of Long-Term Memories00167-8).
